stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .709", "p = .158", "p = 0.661", "p = .147"), Sentence = c("Ratings of repeated life hacks (M = 2.75) were not higher than new ones overall (M = 2.75), F(1, 299) = 0.14, p = .709.", "However, repeated hacks (M = 2.66, SE = 0.02) did not seem any less original than new ones (M = 2.68, SE = 0.02), t(299) = 1.42, p = .158, 95% CI of the mean difference [-0.01, 0.05].", "There was no significant interaction between repetition and judgment type, F(1, 399) = 0.19, p = 0.661.", "Contrary to our predictions, repeated quotes (M = 2.90, SE = 0.03) did not seem truer than new ones (M = 2.86, SE = 0.03), t(199) = 1.46, p = .147, 95% CI of the mean difference [-0.01, 0.09]." )), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. text.text: People often resist innovation.
Maintaining the status quo may involve fluency, or subjective ease of processing.
Content that feels easy to understand seems true, inspires confidence, and is likable.
Across four preregistered experiments (total N = 1002), we investigated whether repeated ideas also seem more creative than new ones.
Participants saw uncommon uses for everyday objects (e.g., rolling out dough with a wine bottle; Experiments 1 -3) or literary quotes (e.g., The richest plan is not to have one; Experiment 4).
Later, they judged the creativity of these ideas and new ones.
Repeated life hacks seemed less creative than new ones, but repeated literary quotes seemed more creative than new ones.
When participants evaluated dimensions of creativity separately, repetition made uses for objects seem more useful without impacting perceived originality.
Our findings support feelings-as-information theory, as people use fluency flexibly in domains like creativity, where novelty should be valued.
Resistance to innovation limits progress in science, policy, and business.
Scientists rejected evidence that misfolded proteins, now called prions, cause neurodegeneration (Zabel & Reid, 2015).
text.formatted: Scientists rejected evidence that misfolded proteins, now called prions, cause neurodegeneration <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Zabel & Reid, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Legislators hesitate to pass bills that give out cash payments, even though they reduce homelessness and generate net societal savings (Dwyer et al., 2023).

text.text: And the founders of Ring -a doorbell camera company that eventually sold for over $1 billion dollars to Amazonleft the popular investment TV show, Shark Tank, without a deal.
The most creative ideas are not always perceived as the best ones.
Uncertainty (Mueller et al., 2012), perceived risk (Keith et al., 2024), and adherence to norms (Reis & Kunde, 2024) undermine support for unconventional ideas.

text.text: Do basic cognitive biases also lead people to reject creative ideas?
People spontaneously evaluate the quality of their own solutions during creative cognition.
Conceiving new ideas involves two phases -generation and evaluation (Kleinmintz et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Conceiving new ideas involves two phases -generation and evaluation <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Kleinmintz et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: We first search for relevant concepts and details in memory, then construct mental images of them (Benedek et al., 2023).

text.text: A participant might search their memory for sturdy, heavy items and remember that they used a brick in place of a stepstool in the past (Ramey & Zabelina, 2024).

text.text: People then select among these candidates by rejecting ones that are typical or impractical, a filtering process that requires cognitive control (Chrysikou, 2019).

text.text: For example, a participant might mentally simulate whether standing on a brick would allow them to reach a kitchen shelf (Orwig et al., 2026).
text.formatted: For example, a participant might mentally simulate whether standing on a brick would allow them to reach a kitchen shelf <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Orwig et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Monitoring our own creative cognition is imperfect.
Participants' ratings of their own solutions correlate with the ratings of independent judges, and more creative individuals are even more likely to identify their best ideas (Silvia, 2008).
text.formatted: Participants' ratings of their own solutions correlate with the ratings of independent judges, and more creative individuals are even more likely to identify their best ideas <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Silvia, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: But when making these inferences, people weigh how the creative process felt.
In moments of insight, solutions come to mind suddenly, with exceptional positive affect, ease, and confidence (Topolinski & Reber, 2010).
text.formatted: In moments of insight, solutions come to mind suddenly, with exceptional positive affect, ease, and confidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Topolinski & Reber, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Solving a difficult problem faster than expected results in a metacognitive prediction error, similar to those associated with unexpected rewards (Dubey et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Solving a difficult problem faster than expected results in a metacognitive prediction error, similar to those associated with unexpected rewards <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Dubey et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These "Aha" moments can be helpful indicators of a solution's actual accuracy (Salvi et al., 2016), but they can also lead to false insights (Danek & Wiley, 2017).

text.text: Errors can also arise when we evaluate the contributions of others.
People who make accurate judgments of their own ideas do not necessarily make accurate judgments of other people's outputs (Runco & Smith, 1992).

text.text: More creative individuals are also better at evaluating the creativity of others' insights (Benedek et al., 2016), even though they still judge their own ideas even more accurately (Guo et al., 2022).

text.text: And more generally, we struggle to appreciate the originality of a highly novel pitch (Licuanan et al., 2007).

text.text: We also are miscalibrated when selecting which solutions to implement.
For example, Blair and Mumford (2007) put participants in decision-making roles for a fictional nonprofit and asked them to choose proposals they would fund.

text.text: Participants passed over risky and more original approaches in favor of ones that provided quick results, aligned more with social norms, and were easy to understand.
This preference for straightforward ideas suggests a role for fluency, or ease of processing.
According to feelings-as-information theory, people often make complex judgments by asking 'How do I feel about this?' (Schwarz, 2012).
text.formatted: According to feelings-as-information theory, people often make complex judgments by asking 'How do I feel about this?' <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Schwarz, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, information that is easy to understand inspires confidence (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973), is better liked (Labroo et al., 2008), feels familiar (Whittlesea, 1993), and seems truer (Fazio et al., 2015).

text.text: Fluency also shapes our perceptions of beauty (Vogel et al., 2020), fame (Jacoby et al., 1989), ethics (Pillai et al., 2023), humor (Gorenz & Schwarz, 2026), and even our own knowledge (Speckmann & Unkelbach, 2024) and mastery of a subject (Miele & Molden, 2010).

text.text: When solving tough problems, feelings of ease can make people overconfident.
For instance, watching an uninformative video of a pilot landing a plane makes people surer that they could land one themselves, though this skill requires extensive training (Jordan et al., 2022).

text.text: Similarly, reading brief survival tips (e.g., yell to bystanders) for "worst case scenarios" (e.g., fall onto subway tracks) inflates participants' feelings of preparation for these situations, suggesting that ease experienced during remembering (i.e., retrieval fluency) misleads us about our own abilities (Brashier et al., 2024).

text.text: One way to make information feel fluent is by repeating it.

For example, repeating statements makes them seem truer than new statements (i.e., illusory truth, Hasher et al., 1977;  see Brashier & Marsh, 2020, for a review); just a single previous exposure boosts credibility (Hassan & Barber, 2021).

text.text: Repeatedly evaluating performance can also inflate judgments.

As examples, judges awarded more favorable scores to performances in later seasons of Dancing with the Stars, and university professors assign higher grades after teaching the same course multiple times (O 'Connor & Cheema, 2018).

text.text: And products that we have seen before also seem more valuable (Greul et al., 2023).

text.text: By definition, people should deem novel ideas to be more creative than repeated ones; creativity reflects both novelty and usefulness (Runco & Jaeger, 2012; Diedrich et al., 2015).

text.text: The current experiments test whether fluency encourages the opposite -ideas that have been encountered before could ironically seem more creative than new ones.
Across four experiments (total N = 1002), participants were initially exposed to a set of ideas, then later judged the creativity of those same ideas as well as new ones.

We investigated whether conflating fluency and creativity depends on depth of processing at exposure (Experiment 2), the specificity of judgments at test (Experiment 3), or the domain that ideas come from (Experiment 4).
One hundred and fifty-one Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk) workers (50 women, M age = 43.57 years) participated for monetary compensation.
An a priori power analysis determined that we would need 54 participants to detect a medium effect with 95% power.
We preregistered and collected a larger sample to account for inattention and noise in online data collection.
This study manipulated repetition within subjects.
We selected 50 uncommon uses for everyday objects (e.g., roll out dough with a wine bottle, see Appendix A).
We divided these ideas into two sets of 25 items.
One set repeated across the exposure and evaluation phases, whereas the other appeared for the first time at evaluation.
Repetition was counterbalanced across participants.
After giving informed consent, participants completed the exposure phase.

We divided these quotes into two sets of 25 items.
One set repeated across the exposure and evaluation phases, whereas the other appeared for the first time at evaluation.

Immediately after exposure, participants completed the evaluation phase.
Participants rated 50 quotes for either creativity on a scale from 1 (very obvious) to 4 (very creative), or truth on a scale from 1 (definitely false) to 4 (definitely true).

We investigated whether fluency explains what we call the novelty penalty, where people reject inventive ideas.
Initially we found the opposite; participants correctly judged repeated life hacks to be less creative than new ones.
A later experiment revealed that repetition impacts two dissociable components of creativity independently.
Fluency inflated participants' perceptions of a life hack's effectiveness but not its originality.
When faced with more subjective literary quotes, participants judged repeated items as more creative, and they intriguingly did not exhibit illusory truth for these claims.
This content is not goal-directed like life hacks are, potentially leaving people to consider their aesthetic appeal instead.
Together, these results suggest that participants used feelings of fluency flexibly when judging creativity, depending on the context.

More broadly, people use heuristics according to their ecological validity (Gigerenzer & Gaissmaier, 2011), relying on a 'fast and frugal' shortcut like fluency only when it outperforms using more information.

text.text: We learn the meanings of heuristics from statistical relationships in the world around us.

For example, people eventually learn that fluency correlates with truth because we are more likely to hear the one true version of a fact (e.g., Neil Armstrong was the first person to walk on the moon) than any of its many possible falsifications (e.g., Buzz Aldrin or Yuri Gagarin).
Crucially, these relationships can be updated with experience.
While items presented in high contrast typically seem familiar because they are easy to read, Unkelbach (2006) reversed this heuristic with feedback.
text.formatted: While items presented in high contrast typically seem familiar because they are easy to read, <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Unkelbach (2006)</ref> reversed this heuristic with feedback.

text.text: Through trial-by-trial learning, participants shifted to indicating that low-contrast names had already been presented.
This pattern generalizes beyond recognition to truth, with participants successfully learning to reinterpret fluent items as false (Unkelbach, 2007).

text.text: In the current experiments, fluency did not inevitably lead to more positive evaluations of ideas, perhaps because people have not learned a clear relationship between creativity and easy processing.
Even when we have learned a given correlation, the source of fluency matters.
People may rely on conceptual, but not perceptual, fluency.
For instance, repetition makes a bad deed seem less immoral (Effron, 2022), but presenting the same actions in higher contrast has no effect (Nadarevic & Kroneisen, 2020).
text.formatted: For instance, repetition makes a bad deed seem less immoral <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Effron, 2022)</ref>, but presenting the same actions in higher contrast has no effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Nadarevic & Kroneisen, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Fluency and familiarity can even be spontaneously discounted when people intentionally disregard easy processing or prior experience as irrelevant (Oppenheimer & Monin, 2009).
text.formatted: Fluency and familiarity can even be spontaneously discounted when people intentionally disregard easy processing or prior experience as irrelevant <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Oppenheimer & Monin, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: As examples, people can ignore stark 'printing errors' (i.e., perceptual disfluency) when deciding the merit of a college admissions essay (Oppenheimer, 2006), disregard the salience (i.e., availability) of famous names when estimating their frequency (Oppenheimer, 2004), and dismiss their ability to recognize the name of a city when judging its size (Oppenheimer, 2003), all when they can attend to a more obvious cue instead.

text.text: Our results suggest that people can make accurate global creativity judgments in the face of fluency, but this may depend on explicitly remembering that they encountered an idea before.

Literary quotes like 'Grief can be a burden but also an anchor' seemed truer with repetition, potentially because they are less tangible and memorable than life hacks like 'pit cherries with a drinking straw.'
Indeed, recollection increases with information's concreteness.

As examples, concrete noun pairs (e.g., diamond/ring; Paivio et al., 1994), adjective-noun pairs (e.g., flaming/forest; Begg, 1972), and short texts (Sadoski et al., 2000) are all better remembered than abstract ones.

text.text: Participants likely recalled reading life hacks like 'rolling out dough with a wine bottle' when they saw them a second time.
Literary quotes are more abstract, potentially leaving people unable to discount in the absence of explicit recollection later.
This content is also more subjective, which reduces the influence of prior exposure.
Repeating socialpolitical opinions like 'Election Day should be a national holiday' does not make them seem more credible (Riesthuis & Woods, 2026).

text.text: Our result identifies another domain in which subjectivity reduces illusory truth.

While fluency is generally an automatic, positive experience that inflates judgments (Winkielman & Cacioppo, 2001), it can also amplify existing judgmental biases in either a positive or negative direction (Landwehr & Eckmann, 2020).

text.text: For instance, while people like abstract patterns the longer they look at them, they ironically like faces less the longer they see them, even though extended exposure increases fluency (Gerger et al., 2017).

text.text: We demonstrated that people use feelings of ease situationally rather than habitually when judging creativity, with small effects of fluency reversing in some contexts.

Our work complements the finding that intuitive assessments of creativity outperform more deliberate ones (Zhu et al., 2017) and suggests that transformative ideas are not devalued due to 'fast and frugal' heuristics.

text.text: If anything, people recognize that an idea that is easy to understand is not necessarily more inventive, so long as it serves a tangible goal.
